clinicalPearls: A family of mesenchymal tumours composed of distinctive perivascular epithelioid cells showing dual melanocytic and smooth-muscle (myoid) differentiation
Co-expresses melanocytic markers (HMB-45, Melan-A, MiTF) and myoid markers (smooth muscle actin, desmin), a combination that is essentially diagnostic
Most cases are linked to inactivation of TSC1 or TSC2 with downstream activation of the mTOR pathway; a distinct subset harbours TFE3 gene rearrangement
The PEComa family includes angiomyolipoma, pulmonary and lymph-node lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) and clear cell sugar tumour, and is associated with the tuberous sclerosis complex
Occurs across many sites including uterus, retroperitoneum, gastrointestinal tract, soft tissue and viscera, with a female predominance overall
Malignancy is predicted by features such as large size, high mitotic activity, necrosis, marked atypia and infiltrative growth, using recognised risk-stratification criteria
mTOR inhibition (for example sirolimus or related agents) is an effective targeted treatment in advanced or malignant TSC-associated disease
reference.pathophysiology: PEComas arise from perivascular epithelioid cells that uniquely coexpress melanocytic and smooth-muscle phenotypes. In most tumours, loss of TSC1 or TSC2 removes inhibition of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), driving unregulated growth and providing the rationale for mTOR-inhibitor therapy. A separate molecular subset is defined by TFE3 rearrangement, which activates a transcription factor programme and tends to occur in younger patients without a tuberous sclerosis background. The shared histology and immunophenotype unite the family despite these distinct genetic mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Angiomyolipoma and other members of the PEComa family
Smooth muscle tumours such as leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma and other clear cell neoplasms
Alveolar soft part sarcoma, particularly in TFE3-driven cases
Adrenocortical or other clear cell visceral tumours
additionalInvestigations: Immunohistochemistry for melanocytic markers (HMB-45, Melan-A) and myoid markers (SMA, desmin)
TFE3 immunohistochemistry and FISH in tumours suggesting the rearranged subset
Molecular testing for TSC1/TSC2 alterations where relevant to therapy
Assessment for stigmata of tuberous sclerosis complex, including renal angiomyolipomas and pulmonary LAM
Cross-sectional imaging to define the primary tumour and detect metastases
Application of malignancy risk-stratification criteria based on size, mitoses, necrosis and atypia
redFlags: Large tumour with high mitotic count, necrosis or marked nuclear atypia indicating malignant potential
Metastatic disease, most often to lung, liver or bone
Features of tuberous sclerosis complex requiring wider evaluation
Retroperitoneal haemorrhage from a large angiomyolipoma-type lesion
reference.prognosis: Many PEComas are benign and cured by complete excision, but malignant tumours defined by adverse histological features can recur and metastasise; advanced and malignant TSC-associated disease often responds to mTOR inhibition, which has substantially improved outcomes for patients with unresectable or metastatic tumours.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing PEComa as metastatic melanoma because of HMB-45 positivity, without recognising the myoid coexpression
Overlooking the diagnosis in visceral or uterine sites where smooth muscle tumours are expected
Failing to consider a TFE3-rearranged PEComa in a younger patient with epithelioid clear cell morphology
Not evaluating for tuberous sclerosis complex when a PEComa or angiomyolipoma is found
Assuming all PEComas are benign and omitting risk stratification
